entries.name: Nuclear fission
entries.desc: Nuclear fission is a reaction in which the nucleus of an atom splits into two or more smaller nuclei, releasing a very large amount of energy; it was discovered in Berlin in December 1938, when the chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium among the products of uranium bombarded with neutrons. Lise Meitner and Otto Robert Frisch explained the result in January 1939, and Frisch named the process after the division of living cells. The extra neutrons it releases make a chain reaction possible, the basis of nuclear power and nuclear weapons.

entries.name: Cell theory
entries.desc: Cell theory is the scientific theory that living organisms are made up of cells, that the cell is their basic unit, and that all cells come from pre-existing cells; it was first formulated in 1839 by Matthias Jakob Schleiden for plants and Theodor Schwann for animals. It built on the microscope, with which Robert Hooke had first described cells, in cork, in 1665. Rudolf Virchow added the third tenet, "Omnis cellula e cellula", in 1855, completing the classical theory, though Robert Remak had already proposed the idea.

entries.name: Soap
entries.desc: Soap is a salt of a fatty acid, often made by mixing fats or oils with an alkali, used for washing and cleaning; the earliest recorded evidence of soap-like materials comes from Mesopotamia, c. 2800 BCE. A Sumerian clay tablet of c. 2500 BCE gives a formula of oil and wood ash for washing woollen clothing. These proto-soaps differed from true soap, which foams; who first made true soap is uncertain, and Pliny the Elder called it "an invention of the Gauls". In the Islamic Golden Age soap-making became an established industry.

entries.name: Maya blue
entries.desc: Maya blue is a turquoise or azure blue pigment made by cultures of pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, such as the Maya and Aztecs, from about 800 CE; it combines indigo dye from the leaves of the anil plant with palygorskite, a natural clay. Found on murals, ceramics, sculptures and codices, it resists weathering: murals at Chichén Itzá, Bonampak and Cacaxtla in Mexico have kept their colour for more than 1,000 years. It was still used in 16th-century convents of colonial Mexico; a recipe to reproduce it was published in 1993.

entries.name: Distillation
entries.desc: Distillation is the separation of the substances in a liquid mixture by selective boiling and the condensation of the vapours in a still; Akkadian tablets of c. 1200 BCE describing perfumery show that a primitive form was known to the Babylonians of Mesopotamia. Baked clay stills of the early centuries CE have been found at Taxila and other sites in Pakistan and India, and alchemists in Roman Alexandria used it in the 1st century CE. Medieval Muslim chemists distilled wine, and in 1500 Hieronymus Brunschwig published the first book devoted to the subject.

entries.name: Alchemy
entries.desc: Alchemy is a philosophical and protoscientific tradition whose common aims were turning base metals into gold and making an elixir of immortality; in its Western form it is first attested in texts written in Greco-Roman Egypt in the first centuries CE, with Alexandria as its centre. Chinese and Indian alchemy appear to have been mostly independent in their earlier stages. Alchemy reached Latin Europe through translations from Arabic from 1144 onwards, and the Latin tradition played a significant role in the development of early modern chemistry and medicine.

entries.name: Chemical revolution
entries.desc: The chemical revolution was the reformulation of chemistry during the 17th and 18th centuries that culminated in the law of conservation of mass and the oxygen theory of combustion, long credited to the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier. Robert Boyle laid its foundations with a corpuscular philosophy drawn from alchemy, and Joseph Black, Henry Cavendish and Joseph Priestley showed that air is a mixture of gases. Lavoisier, who overthrew the phlogiston theory and stressed precise weighing, published a new nomenclature with colleagues in 1787 and his Traité élémentaire de chimie, its culmination, in 1789.

entries.name: Dynamite
entries.desc: Dynamite is an explosive made of nitroglycerin, an absorbent such as clay or diatomaceous earth, and stabilisers, invented in 1866 by the Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel, who stabilised nitroglycerin with earth from the Elbe near his factory in Hamburg, and patented in 1867. Nitroglycerin, first synthesised by Ascanio Sobrero in 1847, had been too sensitive to shock for commercial use. Dynamite was the first safely manageable explosive stronger than black powder and rapidly gained wide-scale use, though it was never popular in warfare; Nobel named it from the Greek dýnamis, "power".

entries.name: Wöhler synthesis
entries.desc: The Wöhler synthesis is the conversion of ammonium cyanate into urea, described by Friedrich Wöhler in 1828 and often cited as the starting point of modern organic chemistry. Wöhler made urea from several sets of reactants, such as cyanic acid with ammonia. That it brought down vitalism, the theory that organic matter possessed a "vital force", is disputed: the work of John Dalton and Jöns Jacob Berzelius had already convinced chemists that organic and inorganic matter obey the same chemical laws, and vitalism began to lose support only after 1845.

entries.name: Haber process
entries.desc: The Haber process, or Haber–Bosch process, is the main industrial method of making ammonia, combining nitrogen from the air with hydrogen over an iron catalyst; the German chemist Fritz Haber demonstrated it in the laboratory in 1909, and Carl Bosch scaled it up for BASF. The first industrial plant opened at Oppau in 1913, and during the First World War Germany used it to make nitric acid for explosives. Most of its ammonia goes into fertiliser, enabling the world's population to grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by 2018.

entries.name: Nylon
entries.desc: Nylon is a family of synthetic polymers joined by amide links, first made as nylon 66 by Wallace Hume Carothers at the DuPont Experimental Station on 28 February 1935. It was the first commercially successful synthetic thermoplastic polymer: DuPont announced it in 1938, a nylon-bristled toothbrush appeared that year, and nylon stockings, on general sale from 1940, sold 64 million pairs in their first year. In response, Paul Schlack of IG Farben developed nylon 6 in 1938. In the Second World War nearly all nylon went into parachutes and other military uses.

entries.name: Kerosene
entries.desc: Kerosene, also called paraffin, is a combustible hydrocarbon liquid distilled from petroleum and used as a fuel for lamps, stoves and jet engines; the distilling of crude oil into kerosene was first written about in the 9th century by the Persian scholar Rāzi. The modern industry began with lamp oil from coal: Abraham Gesner coined the name for a fuel he claimed to have demonstrated in 1846, and James Young patented his paraffin oil in 1850. After Edwin Drake's well of 1859, American refiners switched to petroleum, and kerosene largely replaced whale oil.

entries.name: Trepanning
entries.desc: Trepanning, or trepanation, is a surgical intervention in which a hole is drilled or scraped into the human skull, perhaps the oldest surgical procedure with archaeological evidence; at a burial site in France dated to 6500 BCE, 40 of 120 skulls had trepanation holes. More than 1,500 trephined skulls of the Neolithic period have been found in Europe, Siberia, China and the Americas, and many show that the patient survived. Performed with tools of stone, obsidian, bronze or bone, it was described by Hippocrates and Galen and survives in modern craniotomy.

entries.name: Edwin Smith Papyrus
entries.desc: The Edwin Smith Papyrus is an ancient Egyptian medical text and the oldest known surgical treatise on trauma, copied c. 1600 BCE, probably at Thebes, from an original that may date from the Old Kingdom. Written in hieratic on a scroll 4.68 metres long, it sets out 48 cases of injury, each with examination, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment, and largely avoids magic. Named after the American Egyptologist who bought it in Luxor in 1862, it has been kept at the New York Academy of Medicine since 1948.

entries.name: Hippocratic Corpus
entries.desc: The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of around 60 early Greek medical works associated with the physician Hippocrates, most written in the last decades of the 5th century BCE and the first half of the 4th; none is proven to be his own. Composed in Ionic Greek by many authors, from both the Coan and the Cnidian schools, the treatises explain disease by natural causes rather than divine ones, through the four humours. The corpus includes the Hippocratic Oath and was first printed as a whole, in Latin, in 1525.

entries.name: Acupuncture
entries.desc: Acupuncture is a practice of traditional Chinese medicine in which thin needles are inserted into the body, believed to have originated in China around 100 BCE, when the Huangdi Neijing first documented a system of diagnosis and treatment for it. Gold and silver needles from the tomb of Liu Sheng, of the same period, may be its earliest archaeological trace. It spread to Korea in the 6th century CE, then to Japan and Europe; Willem ten Rhijne coined the term in 1683. Trials and reviews generally find no good evidence of benefit.

entries.name: Bimaristan
entries.desc: A bimaristan is a hospital of the medieval Islamic world; the first true one was probably founded in Baghdad under the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, and the first documented general hospital arose there in 805. Funded by charitable endowments (waqf), bimaristans admitted patients regardless of religion or gender, kept separate wards and written patient records, and trained physicians in lecture halls and on the wards. Later foundations included the Al-Nuri Hospital in Damascus (1156) and the Al-Mansuri Hospital in Cairo (1284), which could hold 8,000 beds.

entries.name: The Canon of Medicine
entries.desc: The Canon of Medicine is an encyclopedia of medicine in five books compiled by Ibn Sina (Avicenna), begun in Gorganj and completed in Hamadan in 1025. It sets out the medical knowledge of the Islamic world, shaped by Greco-Roman medicine, particularly Galen, and by Persian, Chinese and Indian medicine, listing about 800 simple drugs and 650 compound ones. Translated into Latin, it became the standard textbook in European universities into the early modern period and was still taught in Padua as late as 1715.

entries.name: Quarantine
entries.desc: Quarantine is a restriction on the movement of people, animals and goods to prevent the spread of disease or pests; a 30-day isolation of newcomers, the trentino, was first imposed by the Republic of Ragusa (modern Dubrovnik, Croatia) in 1377 to keep out the Black Death. In 1448 the Venetian Senate extended the wait to 40 days, the quarantena that gave the practice its name and proved an effective way of handling plague. In the 1830s Egypt and the Ottoman Empire set up permanent quarantines across the eastern Mediterranean on the western model.

entries.name: De humani corporis fabrica
aka: De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem
On the Fabric of the Human Body
entries.desc: De humani corporis fabrica is a set of seven books on human anatomy by Andreas Vesalius, based on his lectures at Padua and printed by Johannes Oporinus in Basel in 1543. Its more than 250 woodcut illustrations, generally attributed to the studio of Titian, surpassed those of earlier anatomical atlases. Working from human bodies rather than the animal cadavers Galen had used, Vesalius corrected about 300 of Galen's errors, though he kept some, such as different kinds of blood in veins and arteries. More than 700 copies of the 1543 and 1555 editions survive.

entries.name: De Motu Cordis
aka: Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus
entries.desc: De Motu Cordis is William Harvey's treatise on the motion of the heart and blood, first published in 1628, which established that the blood circulates through the body. Treating the heart as a pump and measuring the blood it sends out, Harvey concluded that the same blood keeps returning in a closed circuit, out through the arteries and back by the veins. He had presented the case in lectures by 1616; in 1660 Marcello Malpighi saw blood moving in the capillaries, supplying the missing link in the proof.

entries.name: Quinine
entries.desc: Quinine is an alkaloid from the bark of the cinchona tree, native to Peru, used to treat malaria; extracts of the bark were used against malaria from at least 1632, and the substance itself was first isolated in 1820 by the French researchers Pierre Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Bienaimé Caventou. Cinchona bark, known as Jesuit's bark or Peruvian bark, became one of the most valuable goods shipped from Peru to Europe. Quinine remained the antimalarial drug of choice until the 1940s and played a significant role in the European colonisation of Africa.

entries.name: Variolation
entries.desc: Variolation was the deliberate infection of a person with material from a smallpox patient, usually rubbed into scratches in the skin or, in China, blown up the nose as powdered scabs, to cause a mild illness that gave immunity; its oldest documented use was in 16th-century China. Only 1–2% of those variolated died, against 30% of those who caught smallpox naturally. Practised also in India, Africa and the Ottoman Empire, it reached England and North America in the 1720s and was replaced by Edward Jenner's safer cowpox vaccine after 1796.

entries.name: Smallpox vaccine
entries.desc: The smallpox vaccine is the first vaccine developed against a contagious disease: in 1796 the British physician Edward Jenner showed that infection with the mild cowpox virus gave immunity to smallpox; his Inquiry of 1798 presented cowpox inoculation as a safe alternative to variolation. The word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow. Passed from arm to arm and later grown on calves, the vaccine served the WHO's global campaign of 1958–1977 that eradicated smallpox, the only human disease to be eradicated.

entries.name: General anaesthesia
entries.desc: General anaesthesia is a drug-induced loss of consciousness from which a patient cannot be roused even by pain; the first successful surgery on record under it was performed by the Japanese surgeon Hanaoka Seishū on 14 November 1804. Attempts to produce it appear in the writings of ancient peoples from the Sumerians to the Chinese. Together with antiseptic technique, its development in the 19th century allowed the transition to modern surgery, which pain had made a last resort, and in the 20th century tracheal intubation, monitoring and new agents made it safer.

entries.name: Antiseptic surgery
entries.desc: Antiseptic surgery is the use in operations of antiseptics, substances applied to living tissue to reduce the risk of infection; some French surgeons adopted carbolic acid for it about a decade after Ignaz Semmelweis showed, in 1847–1848, that hand washing before delivery reduced puerperal fever. Cutting surgical infection rates, the practice spread to Italy in the 1860s. In 1867 Joseph Lister explained such results by Louis Pasteur's germ theory and popularised antiseptic methods in the English-speaking world.

entries.name: Pasteurisation
entries.desc: Pasteurisation is the preservation of foods such as milk and fruit juice by mild heat, usually below 100 °C, to kill pathogens and extend shelf life; it is named after the French chemist Louis Pasteur, who found in 1864, at Arbois, that briefly heating young wine to about 50–60 °C killed its microbes and stopped it turning sour with age. Heating wine for preservation had been known in China since 1117. First used for wine and beer, pasteurisation was applied to milk later, and New York City made it compulsory for milk in 1910.

entries.name: Aspirin
entries.desc: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, a drug that reduces pain, fever and inflammation and helps prevent blood clots; the chemist Charles Frédéric Gerhardt first produced it in 1853, and Felix Hoffmann (or perhaps Arthur Eichengrün) of the German company Bayer made it in a pure, stable form in 1897. Its precursor salicin, found in willow bark, has been used for at least 2,400 years. By 1899 Bayer was selling the drug worldwide under the brand name Aspirin; an estimated 40,000 tonnes are consumed each year.

entries.name: ABO blood group system
entries.desc: The ABO blood group system classifies human blood by the presence of the A and B antigens on red blood cells; the Austrian physician Karl Landsteiner discovered it at the University of Vienna, dividing blood into three groups in 1901 after finding that some people's serum clumped others' red cells. His students found a fourth group, later named AB, the following year. It is the most important blood group system for transfusion, since a mismatch can cause a potentially fatal reaction. Landsteiner won the Nobel Prize for it in 1930.

entries.name: Penicillin
entries.desc: Penicillin is a β-lactam antibiotic first obtained from Penicillium moulds; it was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital in London, who saw that mould contaminating a bacterial culture appeared to kill the bacteria. A team led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at the University of Oxford isolated the purified compound in 1940. Mass-produced in the United States, it made a major difference to deaths from infected wounds among Allied forces in the Second World War, and the three men shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.

entries.name: Polio vaccine
entries.desc: Polio vaccines prevent poliomyelitis and come in two types, an inactivated virus given by injection and a weakened virus given by mouth; Hilary Koprowski first tested a live, attenuated oral vaccine successfully in New York in 1950. Jonas Salk's injected vaccine was announced as effective in 1955, after a field trial involving 1.8 million children, and Albert Sabin's oral vaccine came into commercial use in 1961. Since a global eradication effort began in 1988, cases have fallen from an estimated 350,000 a year to 33 in 2018.

entries.name: Oral rehydration therapy
entries.desc: Oral rehydration therapy treats dehydration, especially from diarrhoea, with water containing modest amounts of sugar and salts; the earliest known use was reported by Hemendra Nath Chatterjee in The Lancet in 1953, for patients with mild cholera. It became common after the 1960s finding that glucose promotes the absorption of sodium and water during cholera. During the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971, refugees with cholera given it had a mortality of 3.6%, against 30% with intravenous fluids. It is estimated to lower the risk of death from diarrhoea by up to 93%.

entries.name: Artemisinin
entries.desc: Artemisinin is a drug against malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, discovered in China in 1972 by Tu Youyou in the leaves of sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua). It came out of Project 523, a secret military programme of the People's Liberation Army set up in 1967 that screened a list of nearly 2,000 traditional Chinese medicines; Tu said she was guided by a handbook of 340 CE by Ge Hong. Artemisinin-based combination therapies have become the standard treatment for malaria worldwide, and Tu shared the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery.

entries.name: Coinage
entries.desc: Coinage is the minting of small metal pieces for use as money, first known in the 7th century BCE in China, where a factory at Guanzhuang in Henan made shovel-shaped bronze coins between 640 and 550 BCE, and in Anatolia, where the earliest coins are mostly associated with the kingdom of Lydia. The early Lydian coins were of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver, and King Croesus is credited with the Croeseid, the first true gold coins of standardised purity. Coins spread rapidly in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE.

entries.name: Newspaper
entries.desc: A newspaper is a periodical publication of written news about current events; the German-language Relation, printed from 1605 by Johann Carolus in Strasbourg, in the Holy Roman Empire, is often recognised as the first. Newspapers grew with the spread of the printing press, and within a few decades they could be found in all the major cities of Europe; the first daily, the Einkommende Zeitung, appeared in Leipzig in 1650. Much earlier, the Kaiyuan Za Bao, block-printed government news of Tang dynasty China, is sometimes considered one of the earliest newspapers.

entries.name: Optical telegraph
entries.desc: An optical telegraph is a line of stations, typically towers, that pass text along by visual signals; credit for the first successful one goes to the French engineer Claude Chappe and his brothers in 1792, and Chappe's word télégraphe gave English its 'telegraph'. Operators watched the neighbouring tower through a telescope and passed on the positions of its semaphore arms; the Chappe network came to cover France with 556 stations over 4,800 kilometres. Sweden built the second network, and about half a century later the electrical telegraph replaced such lines.

entries.name: Photography
entries.desc: Photography, whose name means 'drawing of light', is the capture of camera images on light-sensitive materials; the first such image to be fixed was made by the French scientist Nicéphore Niépce in 1826 or 1827, after an exposure of hours or days. His partner Louis Daguerre developed the daguerreotype, the first publicly announced and commercially viable process, whose details were made public in Paris in August 1839. Henry Fox Talbot's developed-out silver halide negative process, which allowed many prints from one negative, remains the basic technology of chemical film cameras.

entries.name: Telephone
entries.desc: The telephone is a device that turns the voice into electrical signals and back into sound at a distance; Johann Philipp Reis demonstrated the first device to transmit a voice by electronic signals before the Physical Society of Frankfurt on 26 October 1861. Credit for the invention is disputed among Reis, Antonio Meucci, Charles Bourseul, Elisha Gray and Alexander Graham Bell, who in March 1876 received the first United States patent for the electric telephone. Bell's patent became the master patent from which others flowed, and switchboards soon linked telephones into exchanges and networks.

entries.name: Radio
entries.desc: Radio is communication by electromagnetic waves sent through the air; after Heinrich Hertz showed in experiments published between 1886 and 1888 that such waves could be transmitted, the Italian inventor Guglielmo Marconi was field testing a wireless system by August 1895 and applied for a British patent in 1896. It was first used for 'wireless telegraphy' in Morse code, and on 12 December 1901 Marconi sent a message across the Atlantic. Audio transmission followed in the early 1900s, and by 1919–1920 regular entertainment broadcasts were heard in The Hague, Buenos Aires and Detroit.

entries.name: Cinematograph
entries.desc: The cinematograph is an early motion-picture machine that served as both film camera and projector; the French inventor Léon Bouly coined the name in a patent of 12 February 1892, and filed for a version that could also project in December 1893. The Lumière brothers filed a patent for their machine, which could also print films, on 13 February 1895, and Louis Lumière first presented a film in Paris on 22 March 1895. After their public screening in December 1895 it became a popular attraction across Europe, the United States, China and India.

entries.name: Television
entries.desc: Television is a medium for transmitting moving images and sound; the first demonstration of the live transmission of images was given by Georges Rignoux and A. Fournier in Paris in 1909, with a matrix of 64 selenium cells. John Logie Baird's transmission of a moving face by radio, shown to members of the Royal Institution by 26 January 1926, is widely regarded as the first true public television demonstration, and Philo Farnsworth's press demonstration of 1928 as the first electronic one. The first regular 'high-definition' service began at Alexandra Palace in 1936.

credit.artist: Radio Corporation of America, Radio City, New York City, NY

entries.name: Analytical Engine
entries.desc: The Analytical Engine is a design for a mechanical general-purpose computer by the English mathematician Charles Babbage, first described in 1837 as the successor to his difference engine. It was to read programs and data from punched cards, a method then used to direct looms such as the Jacquard loom, and its conditional branching, loops and memory make it the first design for a general-purpose computer that could be called Turing-complete. Babbage never completed it; part of the mill built by his son Henry is in the Science Museum in London.

entries.name: ENIAC
entries.desc: ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) was the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer, completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania's Moore School of Electrical Engineering. Designed by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert and financed by the United States Army to calculate artillery firing tables, it was on the order of a thousand times faster than electro-mechanical machines. Six women did most of its programming; it worked at Aberdeen Proving Ground until 1955, and pieces of it are now held by the Smithsonian and other museums.

entries.name: Transistor
entries.desc: A transistor is a semiconductor device that amplifies or switches electrical signals and power; the first working one, a point-contact transistor, was invented in 1947 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, New Jersey. Herbert Mataré and Heinrich Welker invented the point-contact transistor independently in Paris in 1948. Smaller than vacuum tubes and needing less power, transistors made smaller and cheaper radios, calculators and computers possible, and the MOSFET, invented at Bell Labs between 1955 and 1960, became the most widely used type.

entries.name: Integrated circuit
entries.desc: An integrated circuit, or microchip, is an assembly of electronic components such as transistors, resistors and capacitors and their connections, made on a thin piece of semiconductor, usually silicon; Jack Kilby demonstrated the first working example at Texas Instruments on 12 September 1958. About six months later Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor developed the first practical monolithic chip, made of silicon, on which modern chips are based. NASA's Apollo programme was the largest single consumer of integrated circuits between 1961 and 1965, and a modern chip may hold many billions of transistors.

entries.name: ARPANET
entries.desc: The ARPANET (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) was the first wide-area packet-switched network with distributed control, set up by the United States Department of Defense; its first host-to-host connection, between UCLA and the Stanford Research Institute, was made on 29 October 1969. Bob Taylor began the project in 1966 to let researchers share remote computers, and Larry Roberts adopted Donald Davies' concepts for packet switching. In 1973 three-quarters of its traffic was email; it adopted TCP/IP in 1983 and was decommissioned in 1990, having laid the technical foundation of the Internet.

entries.name: World Wide Web
entries.desc: The World Wide Web is a global system of linked documents and other resources shared over the Internet, invented at CERN in 1989 by the English computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee. He submitted his proposal in March 1989 and had a working system by the end of 1990, with a browser called WorldWideWeb and an HTTP server; the Web was released to the whole Internet on 23 August 1991. After CERN made its code available royalty-free in April 1993 and the Mosaic browser appeared, thousands of websites sprang up in less than a year.

entries.name: Mobile phone
entries.desc: A mobile phone is a portable telephone that makes and receives calls over a radio link while its user moves about; the first handheld mobile phone was demonstrated by Martin Cooper of Motorola in New York City on 3 April 1973, with a handset weighing about 2 kilograms. Earlier mobile phones had to be installed in vehicles. Nippon Telegraph and Telephone launched the first cellular network in Japan in 1979, the DynaTAC 8000x of 1983 was the first handheld phone on sale, and by 2024 subscriptions worldwide exceeded 9.1 billion.

entries.name: Awīlum
entries.desc: In the Code of Hammurabi, the Babylonian legal text composed about 1753 BCE, the awīlum was one of three main kinds of person, beside the muškēnum and the slave. The meaning is contested, but the word probably denoted a male member of the higher social class, something like a "gentleman". Under law 215 a physician who healed an awīlum by major surgery took a fee of ten shekels of silver; under law 218 he lost his hand if the patient died. Laws 200 and 202 show that one awīlum could rank above another.

entries.name: Muškēnum
entries.desc: In the Code of Hammurabi, the Babylonian legal text composed about 1753 BCE, the muškēnum was one of three main kinds of person, beside the awīlum and the slave. The meaning is contested, but the word probably denoted a male member of a lower social class, something like a "commoner". The Code did not always treat him more harshly than an awīlum: his life may have been cheaper, but so were some of his fines. As a word for a man of low standing it survives in Arabic miskīn and French mesquin.

entries.name: Kurtaš
entries.desc: Kurtaš was the Elamite word for the workers who drew rations from the Achaemenid Persian administration around Persepolis, recorded in the Persepolis Fortification Tablets of 509–493 BCE. As many women as men appear among them, and some women received more than any man in their group. The word could mean slaves, but in some contexts hired or indentured workers; some studies suggest that Thracians and Greeks with the legal status of kurtaš, paid and fed from the Persian treasury, helped dig Xerxes' canal through the Athos peninsula. From 492 BCE the Treasury tablets record silver paid in place of rations.

entries.name: Metic
entries.desc: A metic was a free resident of classical Athens, or of some other Greek cities, without citizenship there: an immigrant from another polis or a freed slave, allowed to stay indefinitely without political rights. Metics served in the army and, if wealthy, funded liturgies, but could not own land or a house in Attica without a special grant. They paid the metoikion, twelve drachmas a year for a man and his household and six for an independent woman, and a metic convicted of having no citizen sponsor was sold as a slave.

entries.name: Helots
entries.desc: The helots were a subjugated group who formed most of the population of Laconia and Messenia, the territories ruled by Sparta; tied to the land, they farmed it to support the Spartan citizens. Ancient writers disagreed on their status: Critias called them "slaves to the utmost", Pollux put them "between free men and slaves". According to Aristotle, the ephors declared war on them every year, so that Spartans could kill them without religious pollution. Some won freedom by military service, like the 700 who served Brasidas in 424 BCE; freed helots were called neodamodeis.

entries.name: Perioeci
entries.desc: The perioeci, "those dwelling around", were the second-tier citizens of Sparta until about 200 BCE, free people living in several dozen dependent cities, mostly in Laconia and Messenia. These cities ran their own domestic affairs but followed Sparta's foreign policy and sent men to its army, where they fought as hoplites; in the Spartan state they had no say. As Spartan citizens were barred from productive work, the perioeci ran trade and crafts, making the army's weapons and armour, and they alone could travel freely abroad. Like the Spartiates, they owned helots.

entries.name: Dynatoi
entries.desc: The dynatoi, "the powerful", were in Byzantine law the senior ranks of civil, military and church officialdom, usually also holding considerable fortunes and landed estates. In Asia Minor the Phokades and the Maleinoi almost monopolised senior posts in the early and mid-10th century. Emperors from Romanos I Lekapenos to Basil II legislated to protect smaller landowners from them and keep them from the military lands, and Basil II made them liable for the taxes of their poorer neighbours. Their posts were seldom hereditary, but by the mid-11th century a few families formed a hereditary aristocracy.

entries.name: Pronoia
entries.desc: Pronoia, Greek for "care" or "forethought", was a grant of state revenue in the late Byzantine Empire, from the 11th century to the 15th. It transferred imperial fiscal rights, chiefly the taxes of cultivated land, usually for the holder's lifetime; the emperor could revoke it at will. Manuel I Komnenos gave pronoiai to aristocratic officers instead of a salary, and Michael VIII Palaiologos, who recovered Constantinople in 1261, let them be inherited. It carried no specific military obligation, unlike a western fief, and the Ottomans borrowed it for their own timar system.

entries.name: Villein
entries.desc: A villein was a serf of medieval western Europe, tied to the land of a manor, who owed its lord dues and services, including work on his fields, and could not leave without his permission. Villeins paid fines that freemen did not, as when a daughter married a man from another manor, but could own property, unlike slaves. Lords could free them, often for payment. Villeinage declined after the Black Death and had largely died out in England by 1500; in France it lasted until 1789.

entries.name: Thrall
entries.desc: A thrall was a slave or serf in Viking Age Scandinavia, the lowest of the three orders of Norse society, below the freeman (karl) and the nobleman (jarl). Thralls were property, bought and sold; people became thralls by birth, debt, punishment or capture in war. Most captives of Viking raids were sold abroad, many to Muslim merchants for silver and silk; those kept tended animals, fished and farmed. Thralls could be freed or buy their freedom, and slavery was phased out from the 12th century until the last Swedish county abolished it in 1335.

entries.name: Jarl
entries.desc: Jarl was a rank of the nobility in Scandinavia in the Viking Age and early Middle Ages: a chieftain appointed to rule a territory in a king's stead, or a sovereign prince. Jarls ruled several Norwegian petty kingdoms, often with no less power than neighbouring kings; the strongest were the jarls of Lade. In Denmark the jarl was the king's deputy; later Norway and Sweden usually had a single jarl, second only to the king. It gave way to the title of duke; the last jarl in mainland Norway was appointed in 1295.

entries.name: Third Estate
entries.desc: The Third Estate was the order of commoners, peasants and bourgeoisie alike, in the three estates of medieval and early modern Europe; in France under the ancien régime it made up over 98 per cent of the population. Free peasants paid disproportionately high taxes, while nobles were exempt from the taille, France's oldest direct tax. Moving to another estate was extremely rare. In 1789 its deputies to the Estates General, joined by the lower clergy, held out for their right to representation, and on 17 June the assembly was reconstituted as the National Assembly.

entries.name: Sosloviye
entries.desc: Sosloviye was the term for the legal estates of the Russian Empire, introduced in the 18th and 19th centuries to approximate Europe's estates of the realm. The Code of Laws of 1832 defined four: the nobility and the clergy, who paid no personal tax, and the town-dwellers and the peasants, who did; the peasants, the great majority, supplied the army's conscripts. The inorodtsy, non-Russian peoples of Siberia, Central Asia and the Caucasus, were treated apart. After serfdom was abolished the estates no longer matched society, but the terms lasted until the revolution of 1917.

entries.name: Awlad al-nas
entries.desc: Awlad al-nas, "sons of respectable people", was the name for the sons of mamluks in the Mamluk Sultanate, which ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1517. Born free and Muslim, they were excluded from the closed military caste their fathers had joined. Only men who had grown up outside Muslim lands and entered service as slaves, to be converted, trained in barracks and freed, could join it. The awlad al-nas served instead in scribal and administrative posts or as commanders of the halqa, troops who were not mamluks.

entries.name: Reaya
entries.desc: The reaya, or rayah, were the tax-paying lower class of Ottoman society, as distinct from the askeri, the military class, and the kul, slaves including the Janissaries. The term was used for the tax-paying peasant subjects of the timariots, and an Ottoman principle held that "the son of a rayah is a rayah". Christian reaya faced legal and religious discrimination and paid a land tax and a poll tax on non-Muslims, the haraç and the cizye; by the end of the 18th century the word had come to mean Christians.

credit.artist: MacKenzie, G. Muir (Georgina Muir), d. 1874; Irby, A. P. (Adelina Paulina), 1833-1911

entries.name: Jati
entries.desc: Jati is the term traditionally used in the Indian subcontinent for a cohesive group such as a caste, sub-caste, clan, tribe or religious sect, often translated approximately as "caste". A person is born into a jati and marries within it; traditionally each was regulated by a caste council and followed a hereditary occupation, exchanging services and produce with others. Many of these thousands of groups straddled two or more varnas, but the British census from 1901 fitted each into one. Madhav Gadgil wrote that the system had been fully crystallised for at least 1,500 years.

entries.name: Vaishya
entries.desc: Vaishya is the third of the four varnas of the Vedic Hindu social order in India, ranked below the Brahmins and the Kshatriyas, whom it traditionally had the duty to sustain or patronise. Hindu texts, among them the Bhagavad Gita, assigned Vaishyas agriculture, the care of cattle and trade, but over time they came to be landowners, traders and money-lenders. With the Brahmins and Kshatriyas they claim dvija, "twice-born", status after the sacrament of initiation. The historian Ram Sharan Sharma described the Gupta Empire as a Vaishya dynasty.

entries.name: Zamindar
entries.desc: A zamindar was the holder of an estate, a zamindari, in the Indian subcontinent, typically hereditary and with the right to collect taxes; the Persian word for landowner came into use under the Mughal Empire. The word covered autonomous chiefs, two to three hundred under Akbar by one contemporary count, and intermediaries who collected revenue from the peasants but did not own the land. The East India Company's Permanent Settlement of 1793 made zamindars proprietors for a fixed annual rent, and land reforms in India and Pakistan abolished the system in the 1950s.

entries.name: Yangban
entries.desc: The yangban were the ruling class of Joseon Korea, educated aristocrats and scholar-officials named for the "two branches" of office, civil (munban) and military (muban). Office came by law through the state examinations (gwageo), but only yangban families could afford the years of study they required. Locally the status was hereditary in all but law: lineages were listed in registers (hyangan) whose householders sat on a local council, and in the 17th and 18th centuries a few grandee families based in Seoul or the Han River valley monopolised high office. The legal status was abolished in 1894.

entries.name: Nobi
entries.desc: The nobi were the enslaved class of Goryeo and Joseon Korea, legally the lowest rank, who could be bought, sold or given away; at their peak, in the mid-Joseon period, they were over 30 per cent of the population. Status was mostly hereditary, the child of a nobi and a commoner usually taking the lower one. Most lived apart from their owners with houses, families and land, but their property reverted to the owner at death. Nobi caught fleeing were severely punished, and an owner was not held responsible if one died of the beating.

entries.name: Cheonmin
entries.desc: The cheonmin, the "base" or lowborn people, were the lowest class of Korean society under the Goryeo (918–1392) and Joseon (1392–1897) dynasties, set apart in law from the free "good people" (yangin). Their status was largely hereditary and tied to work the upper classes thought unclean: butchers, shamans, shoemakers, metalworkers, jailers, prostitutes and performers such as the gisaeng entertainers were cheonmin, and the nobi, the enslaved servants of the yangban and the royal family, were taken from among them. They were barred from government service and the civil service examinations and lived segregated from the rest of society.

entries.name: Hyakushō
entries.desc: The hyakushō, the peasants, came second in shinōkōshō, the Confucian scheme of four occupations adopted from China: samurai, peasants, craftsmen and merchants. In Tokugawa Japan peasants were the great majority of the people, usually put at about 80 per cent, under a hereditary samurai class of about 5 per cent. Older scholars read the scheme as a ranking, but studies since about 1995 have found that peasants, craftsmen and merchants were equal beneath the samurai, a classification rather than a pecking order, and the old hierarchy chart has been removed from Japanese history textbooks.

entries.name: Hinin
entries.desc: The hinin, literally "non-humans", were an outcast group of Edo-period Japan (1603–1868), placed with the kawata (called eta in official documents, a term now a slur) outside the social hierarchy. They were made to beg, perform in the streets and bury executed criminals, work deemed polluting, and they cleaned the towns, nursed the sick and worked in prisons. The status was hereditary, but the poor and offenders could fall into it: under the Edo law code, the survivor of a couple's attempted suicide became hinin. Unlike the kawata, hinin could under some conditions rejoin the commoners, as when relatives paid, and the status was abolished in 1871.

entries.name: Nyamakala
entries.desc: The nyamakala are the hereditary, endogamous occupational castes of the Sudano-Sahelian peoples of West Africa, above all the Mandinka. Mandinka nyamakala include the griots (jeli), the smiths and carpenters (numu), the leatherworkers and weavers (garanke) and the singers of Islamic praise (fune). The name joins nyama, 'vital force', and kala, 'handle': any craft that handled the vital force of nature was nyamakala. Once a term for any talented people, it came to mark a lowly status below the nobles and the freeborn as slavery and social stratification grew with the jihads and colonial rule.

entries.name: Pipiltin
entries.desc: The pipiltin (singular pilli) were the hereditary nobles of the Mexica, or Aztec, Empire. Some sources describe them as the children of rulers and lords (tlatoque and teteuctin); in a narrower sense the word named the lowest rank of the hereditary nobility, above commoners raised to noble status for an outstanding deed in war. They claimed descent from the Toltecs and from the Aztecs' original migrant founders, which entitled them to goods and dwellings fitting their rank. Pipiltin served as ambassadors and ministers and in the army and priesthood, often heading noble houses (tecalli) with their own lands and dependent labourers, and their children studied at the calmecac.

entries.name: Macehualtin
entries.desc: The macehualtin (singular macehualli) were the commoners of Aztec society, most of them farmers working land that belonged to their calpolli, which a family kept as long as it did not lie fallow for more than two years. They grew maize, beans and squash and paid tribute from their produce to the nobility. Their children attended the telpochcalli from the age of fifteen, and taking captives in war offered a commoner the one slim chance of rising into the nobility. Moctezuma II (1502–1520) widened the divide, barring them from service in the royal palaces.

entries.name: Ajaw
entries.desc: Ajaw, 'lord', is a Maya political title known from pre-Columbian inscriptions, used for any of the leading nobles of a polity. Because the ajaw performed religious rites, it also designated a member of the priesthood, while k'uhul ajaw, 'divine lord', marked a polity's sovereign, even one who in theory acknowledged an overlord. For women rulers such as K'awiil Ajaw of Coba the title was sometimes prefixed with Ix, 'woman'. A tomb at K'o, near Holmul in Guatemala, dated 350–300 BCE and possibly royal, holds the earliest evidence of the institution in the Maya Lowlands.

entries.name: Kuraka
entries.desc: A kuraka, or curaca, was an Andean aristocrat and magistrate who headed an ayllu or a federation of ayllus, an office often but not always inherited; under the Inca Empire his authority was granted by the Inca. Kurakas collected taxes, allocated farmland, settled disputes, judged minor crimes and chose wives for unmarried men of 25 or over, and were exempt from taxation, with the right to several wives and to ride in a litter. Under Spanish rule they mobilised tribute and labour, and a kuraka, Tupac Amaru II, led the Andean rebellion of 1780–1781.

entries.name: Ayllu
entries.desc: The ayllu is the traditional community of the Andes, especially among the Quechua and Aymara: a network of families, often with a putative or fictive common ancestor, holding a territory in common. Ayllus predate the Inca conquest and still exist, particularly in Bolivia and Peru. Under the Incas, largely self-sufficient ayllus relied on the state storehouses only in disasters such as El Niño years. Members owed one another reciprocal help (ayni) and communal work (mink'a), and paid the mit'a, labour owed as tax to the Inca state and later to the Spanish viceroyalties.

entries.name: Aclla
entries.desc: The acllas, the 'chosen women' of the Inca Empire, were taken as tribute from the provinces at eight to ten years old, mostly from families of rank. In houses of chosen women (acllawasi) they trained for about four years in religion, weaving, cooking and brewing chicha. Some then lived out their lives in religious service; others became wives of men who had served the empire, or secondary wives of the emperor, and a few were sacrificed in the capacocha rite. Acllas had to remain celibate on pain of death, and their families rose in standing.

entries.name: Casta
entries.desc: Casta, Spanish and Portuguese for 'lineage', was a label of descent and standing in colonial Spanish America, chiefly for people of mixed Spanish, Indigenous and African ancestry. The basic mixed categories in official documents were mestizo, generally the child of a Spaniard and an Indigenous person, and mulatto, of a Spaniard and a black African. Spaniards and mestizos paid no tribute and could be ordained; free black people, Indigenous people and other castas paid tribute and were barred from the priesthood. Historians now question whether a rigid 'caste system' existed: the casta paintings of the 18th century, which set many mixtures out in a fixed order under labels rarely used in practice, may have been an attempt to order a more fluid reality.

entries.name: Peninsulares
entries.desc: Peninsulares were Spaniards born in Spain who lived in the empire's possessions overseas, in the Americas, the Spanish East Indies or Spanish Guinea. Higher offices in Spanish America and the Philippines were held by peninsulares, who were distinguished from the criollos, Spaniards born in the New World, and from the insulares born in the Philippines. In some places and times, as during the wars of independence, they were called godos, 'Goths', in scorn, or in Mexico gachupines; godos is still used pejoratively for Spaniards in Chile and for peninsular Spaniards in the Canary Islands.

entries.name: Gens de couleur libres
entries.desc: Gens de couleur libres, 'free people of colour', was the name used in France's Caribbean colonies before the abolition of slavery for free people of African descent, mostly of mixed African and European ancestry. In Saint-Domingue, where about 16,000 were free before 1793, they owned about a third of the land and a quarter of the enslaved people by the late colonial period. Though nominally equal under the Code Noir, they lacked the rights of Frenchmen, notably the vote, and their demand for equal rights became an early central issue of the Haitian Revolution.

entries.name: Grands blancs
entries.desc: The grands blancs, "big whites", were the small, exclusive white elite at the top of the French colony of Saint-Domingue, many of them nobles, most of whom lived in France or had been born there. They held most of the power and much of the property, including the 800 large sugar plantations, the most valuable in the colony: the average sugar plantation worked 300 enslaved people, while petits blancs and free people of colour owned 11,700 smaller plantations. Sugar planting was costly and often left its owner deep in debt. In 1791, within two months of the rising in the north, enslaved rebels burned 280 sugar plantations of the grands blancs.

entries.name: Aliʻi
entries.desc: The aliʻi were the hereditary nobility of the Hawaiian Islands, the higher and lesser chiefs, men and women alike, who were believed to descend from the gods. Each of the four largest islands usually had its own aliʻi nui, or supreme high chief; mōʻī, first borne by Maui's highest chief, was later used for all rulers of the islands. The highest born, the nīʻaupiʻo, came of unions between siblings or other close kin. Aliʻi kept a role in government until 1893, when Queen Liliʻuokalani was overthrown in a coup backed by the United States.

entries.name: Makaʻāinana
entries.desc: The makaʻāinana were the commoners of ancient Hawaiʻi, who farmed, fished and practised the simpler crafts, labouring for their families and to support the chiefs (aliʻi) and priests (kahuna). In Hawaiian belief all land belonged to the gods; the chiefs managed it and controlled the commoners who worked it. When a chief died or was defeated the lands were shared out anew, but commoners were usually left in their houses and fields, paying tribute and labour to the new chief under a new overseer (konohiki). Beneath them were only the kauwā: servants, slaves and outcasts.

entries.name: Absolute monarchy
entries.desc: Absolute monarchy concentrated all power in a hereditary ruler answerable, in theory, to God alone. Justified by Bodin, Hobbes and the doctrine of divine right, it built the armies, bureaucracies and courts of early modern Europe, from Louis XIV’s France to Frederick the Great’s Prussia, before revolutions between 1688 and 1917 replaced it with constitutional government almost everywhere.

entries.name: Tyranny (ancient Greece)
entries.desc: Greek tyranny was the rule of one man who seized power in a city-state outside its traditional order. Between the 7th and 2nd centuries BCE tyrants such as Cypselus, Peisistratus and Dionysius I brought prosperity, building and war but rarely founded lasting dynasties, and their enemies, from Athenian democrats to Plato and Aristotle, made the tyrant the enduring image of lawless power.

entries.name: Dictatorship
entries.desc: Dictatorship began as a lawful Roman office, supreme power granted for a single emergency and surrendered when it passed. In the modern world the word came to mean rule without legal limits or free elections, by soldiers, single parties or one man; it was the form under which many of the 20th century’s mass killings took place, and it remains common today.

entries.name: Aristocracy
entries.desc: Aristocracy, rule by a privileged few who claimed to be the best, governed much of the world from the early Greek city-states to the First World War, usually as a hereditary landed nobility. Its defenders saw it as a school of experience and a check on kings and crowds, its critics as privilege and exclusion.

entries.name: Oligarchy
entries.desc: Oligarchy, rule by a few, usually the rich, was the commonest constitution of the Greek city-states and reached its most enduring form in the Republic of Venice, governed by a closed patriciate from 1297 to 1797.

entries.name: Theocracy
entries.desc: Theocracy is government in the name of God, by priests, a sacred ruler or religious law. Named by Josephus for ancient Judea, it took forms as different as the Papal States, Tibet under the Dalai Lamas and the Islamic Republic of Iran.

entries.name: Military junta
entries.desc: A military junta is government by a council of officers, usually after a coup. Korea’s Goryeo generals ruled this way from 1170, and juntas spread across Latin America, Africa, Asia and southern Europe after 1945.

entries.name: One-party state
entries.desc: The one-party state, in which a single party monopolises power, emerged in Soviet Russia after 1917 and became the form of communist, fascist and many post-colonial regimes. Its defenders claimed unity, stability and development; its record includes famines, terror and stagnation as well as rapid industrialisation.

entries.name: Direct democracy
entries.desc: Direct democracy is government by the citizens themselves rather than by their representatives. Classical Athens, which ruled itself through an assembly, a council and juries chosen by lot from 508 to 322 BCE, gave it its name and its first defenders and critics; today it lives on in the Swiss open-air assemblies and in the referendums and initiatives of Switzerland, many US states and other countries.

entries.name: Parliamentary democracy
entries.desc: Parliamentary democracy is government by ministers drawn from and answerable to an elected parliament, which can remove them by withdrawing its confidence. Growing out of 18th-century British cabinet government under Robert Walpole and spread through the British Empire and across Europe, it now prevails in most of Europe and the Commonwealth, praised for flexibility and accountability and criticised for unstable coalitions and weak checks.

entries.name: Presidential democracy
entries.desc: Presidential democracy is government by a president elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term, under a constitution that separates and balances powers.

entries.name: Republic
entries.desc: A republic is a state without a monarch, governed as the public’s affair by officials elected for limited terms under law. Born by tradition in Rome in 509 BCE, revived by the city-states of medieval Italy and by the Dutch, and spread by the American and French revolutions, it was usually run by elites before the 19th century and is now the most common form of state.

entries.name: Chiefdom
entries.desc: The chiefdom was the form in which many farming and fishing peoples first lived under permanent rulers: a hereditary chief at the head of ranked kin, fed by tribute and upheld by ritual rather than by officials.

entries.name: Nomadic confederation
entries.desc: The nomadic confederation was the steppe’s answer to the farming empires on its edges: herding tribes joined under one ruling clan and khan, organised as a single army and sustained by plunder, tribute and trade.

entries.name: City-state
entries.desc: The city-state, a city that governs itself and its countryside, was among the earliest forms of state and one of the most inventive. From Uruk and Athens to Kilwa, Venice and Lübeck it fostered citizenship, commerce and republican thought, though its small size left it prone to faction and conquest; Singapore, Monaco and Vatican City carry it on today.

entries.name: Colonial rule
entries.desc: Colonial rule, the government of territories and peoples by distant states as subjects rather than citizens, carried European power across the world from 1415 and shaped its borders, languages, economies and states.

entries.name: Chollima on the Wing
entries.desc: "Chollima on the Wing" is a North Korean song made to stir popular support for the Chollima Movement, the state's first and best-known mass mobilisation campaign. The Chollima of its title is the winged horse of East Asian legend, the qianlima of the Chinese classics, said to be too swift to be ridden by any mortal and named for its ability to cover a thousand li in a single day.

entries.name: Chollima Movement
entries.desc: The Chollima Movement was a state-sponsored mass mobilisation campaign in North Korea, launched in 1956 or 1958 to speed economic development through ideological incentives to work harder and the personal guidance of Kim Il Sung rather than economic management. It took its name from the winged horse of East Asian legend, said to cover a thousand li in a day, which Kim Il Sung first invoked in December 1956 before the five-year plan of 1957 to 1961; workers who surpassed their targets were named Chollima riders, and from 1959 the Chollima Work Team Movement set teams competing for production titles. The plan’s aims were met within four years, but at the cost of quality, a distorted economy and an exhausted workforce, and North Korea has never acknowledged the movement’s failures. The winged horse became an icon of the state: the Chollima Statue on Mansu Hill in Pyongyang was unveiled in 1961, and the name has since been given to trucks, a metro line, the national football team and a rocket.

entries.name: Anarchism
entries.desc: Anarchism is a political philosophy and movement that seeks to replace the state, capitalism and all coercive hierarchy with voluntary associations. Taking shape in 19th-century Europe with Proudhon, Bakunin and Kropotkin, it flourished until the Spanish Civil War, was suppressed by the Bolsheviks and defeated by the communists in Spain, and has revived since the 1960s in protest movements.

entries.name: Capitalism
entries.desc: Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership of the means of production, production for profit and the accumulation of capital through competitive markets and wage labour.

entries.name: Communism
entries.desc: Communism is the ideology of a classless, stateless society based on common ownership. Given its modern definition by Marx and Engels in 1848, it took power in Russia in 1917 and later ruled more than a third of the world’s population; its one-party states industrialised and spread literacy, but also carried out purges, famines and repression whose death toll is still debated.

entries.name: Conservatism
entries.desc: Conservatism is a philosophy and ideology that seeks to preserve traditional institutions, customs and values, founded as a modern tradition by Edmund Burke in his opposition to the French Revolution.

entries.name: Feminism
entries.desc: Feminism is a range of movements and ideologies, originating in late 18th-century Europe, which hold that societies are patriarchal and seek the equality of the sexes.

entries.name: Hindutva
entries.desc: Hindutva is the Hindu nationalist ideology that V. D. Savarkar formulated in 1923, defining Hindus as those who hold India their fatherland and holy land. Carried by the RSS from 1925, adopted by the Bharatiya Janata Party in 1989, it has shaped Indian government since 2014; its proponents call it cultural nationalism, while many scholars compare it to fascism; violence motivated by it, above all against Muslims, has risen since the mid-2010s.

entries.name: Imperialism
entries.desc: Imperialism is the maintaining and extending of power over foreign nations. Named in the 19th century, it drove the European empires, joined by the United States and Japan, to conquer and rule much of the world, justified by a civilizing mission and theories of race and enforced with great violence.

entries.name: Islamism
entries.desc: Islamism is a range of movements holding that Islam should shape politics and the state through sharia. Formed by Rashid Rida, Hassan al-Banna, Maududi and Qutb after the end of the Ottoman caliphate, it took power in Iran in 1979 and entered elections across the Muslim world, while militant Salafi jihadists from al-Qaeda to ISIL waged armed jihad; since about 2020 observers have seen it decline.

entries.name: Kemalism
entries.desc: Kemalism is the ideology of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of the Republic of Turkey in 1923, built on six principles: republicanism, populism, nationalism, laicism, statism and reformism. Its reforms abolished the caliphate and Islamic law and remade Turkish society on Western models, inspiring modernizers abroad, while its nationalism long denied Kurdish identity.

entries.name: Liberalism
entries.desc: Liberalism is a political and moral philosophy of individual rights, liberty, consent of the governed and equality before the law, first systematised by John Locke and carried by the revolutions of 1688, 1776 and 1789.

entries.name: Maoism
entries.desc: Maoism, officially Mao Zedong Thought, is Mao Zedong’s adaptation of Marxism–Leninism to agrarian China, built on peasant revolution, people’s war and the mass line.

entries.name: Social democracy
entries.desc: Social democracy is a centre-left ideology that seeks social equality through gradual, democratic reform within a regulated, mostly capitalist economy. Born in the 19th-century labour movement, it parted from communism after 1917 and built the welfare states of post-war Europe; since the 1970s it has contended with neoliberalism, the Third Way and electoral decline.

entries.name: Investiture Controversy
entries.desc: The Investiture Controversy, or Investiture Contest, was a conflict between the Church and the state in medieval Europe over the ability to choose and install bishops, abbots and the Pope himself. It began in 1076 as a power struggle between Pope Gregory VII and Henry IV, then King and later Holy Roman Emperor, and led to nearly 50 years of conflict. It ended in 1122 with the Concordat of Worms, agreed by Pope Callixtus II and Emperor Henry V: bishops swore fealty to the monarch, while the church kept the right to invest them with sacred authority, symbolized by a ring and staff. A struggle between Pope Paschal II and Henry I of England ended in the similar Concordat of London.

entries.name: Young Italy
entries.desc: Young Italy (La Giovine Italia) was an Italian political movement founded by Giuseppe Mazzini in Marseille in July 1831, while he was in exile. It aimed to create a united Italian republic through a general insurrection in the Italian reactionary states and the lands occupied by the Austrian Empire, and had about 60,000 members around 1833. Its revolts in Savoy and Piedmont in 1833 and 1834 and later risings in Sicily, Tuscany and Bologna failed, and many members were arrested and executed. Giuseppe Garibaldi joined it around 1833; it was affiliated with Mazzini's Giovine Europa, and was effectively ended after a last failed revolt against Austria in Milan in 1853.

entries.name: Nika riots
entries.desc: The Nika riots were a revolt against the Byzantine emperor Justinian I in Constantinople over a week in 532. The chariot-racing factions, the Blues and the Greens, united under the cry Nika, or victory, after Justinian refused to pardon two partisans who had survived execution; the rioters demanded the dismissal of John the Cappadocian and Tribonian and proclaimed Hypatius, a nephew of Anastasius I, emperor. Fires destroyed much of the city, including the Hagia Sophia. Troops led by Belisarius and Mundus stormed the Hippodrome, and according to Procopius around 30,000 people were killed; Justinian had Hypatius executed and later rebuilt the Hagia Sophia.

entries.name: Harry S. Truman
entries.desc: Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. Born in rural Missouri, he fought in France as an artillery captain in World War I, was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1934 and, as vice president, succeeded Franklin D. Roosevelt on his death in April 1945. He authorized the first and only use of nuclear weapons in war, against Hiroshima and Nagasaki, set up the Marshall Plan, established the Truman Doctrine and supported the founding of NATO to contain Soviet communism. He presided over the onset of the Cold War, the Berlin Airlift and the Korean War, and issued Executive Order 9981, which desegregated the armed forces.

entries.name: Willy Brandt
entries.desc: Willy Brandt, born Herbert Ernst Karl Frahm in Lübeck, was a German politician who led the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) from 1964 to 1987 and was chancellor of West Germany from 1969 to 1974. He fled to Norway and then Sweden under the Nazi regime, taking the name Willy Brandt as a pseudonym, and first won fame as governing mayor of West Berlin. As chancellor he launched Ostpolitik to improve relations with Eastern Europe, and in 1970 knelt in silence at a memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising; he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971. He resigned in 1974 after his aide Günter Guillaume was exposed as an agent of the Stasi.

entries.name: Paris Commune
entries.desc: The Paris Commune was a French revolutionary government that seized power in Paris on 18 March 1871 and controlled parts of the city until 28 May 1871. After the French Army's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War, soldiers of the National Guard took the city and refused the authority of the Third Republic under Adolphe Thiers. The Commune separated church and state, remitted rents and abolished child labor. The army suppressed it in the semaine sanglante, the bloody week beginning on 21 May, killing in battle or executing an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 Communards; Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels saw it as the first example of the dictatorship of the proletariat.

entries.name: Muslim Brotherhood
entries.desc: The Muslim Brotherhood is a transnational Sunni Islamist organization founded in Egypt in 1928 by the scholar and schoolteacher Hassan al-Banna. It began as a religious and social movement that preached, taught the illiterate and set up hospitals, then entered politics against British colonial rule; its stated aim is a state ruled by Sharia under a caliphate. Members assassinated the prime minister Mahmoud El Nokrashy Pasha in 1948, and Sayyid Qutb promoted takfirism in Milestones (1964); the group abandoned violence in the 1970s. Its candidate Mohamed Morsi became Egypt's first democratically elected president in 2012, but was overthrown in 2013, after which the group was banned in Egypt.

entries.name: Thomas More
entries.desc: Sir Thomas More was an English lawyer, judge, social philosopher, author, statesman, theologian and Renaissance humanist who served Henry VIII as Lord Chancellor from 1529 to 1532. He wrote Utopia, published in 1516, which describes the political system of an imaginary island state, and wrote polemics against Martin Luther, Huldrych Zwingli and William Tyndale. He refused to acknowledge Henry as supreme head of the Church of England, and after refusing to take the Oath of Supremacy he was convicted of treason and executed in 1535. Pope Pius XI canonised him as a martyr in 1935, and Pope John Paul II declared him patron saint of statesmen and politicians in 2000.

entries.name: Dead Sea Scrolls
entries.desc: The Dead Sea Scrolls are a set of ancient Jewish manuscripts from the Second Temple period, discovered between 1946 and 1956, mostly in the Qumran Caves near the Dead Sea in the West Bank. Dating from the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE, they include the oldest surviving manuscripts of entire books later included in the Jewish and Christian biblical canons, texts never canonized, and sectarian writings such as the Community Rule and the War Scroll. Most are in Hebrew, some in Aramaic and a few in Greek; researchers have assembled 981 different manuscripts from 11 caves. Almost all are held in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

entries.name: Jean Bodin
entries.desc: Jean Bodin was a French jurist and political philosopher, a member of the Parlement of Paris and professor of law at the University of Toulouse, who wrote amid the religious conflict in France after the Protestant Reformation. His best-known work, The Six Books of the Republic (1576), defined sovereignty as the absolute and perpetual power of a Republic and favoured a strong national monarchy as an antidote to factional strife. At the Estates-General at Blois he opposed a new war against the Huguenots. He also wrote On the Demonomania of the Sorcerers (1580) and the Colloquium heptaplomeres (1588), a dialogue of seven men of different faiths, and died in Laon during a plague epidemic.

entries.name: Max Weber
entries.desc: Max Weber was a German sociologist, historian, jurist and political economist, one of the central figures in the development of sociology. Born in Erfurt in 1864, he taught in Berlin, Freiburg and Heidelberg, and in The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism argued that the Protestant work ethic influenced the creation of modern capitalism. He defined states by their monopoly on the legitimate use of force within a given area and divided social authority into charismatic, traditional and rational-legal forms. After the First World War he co-founded the German Democratic Party and advised the drafting of the Weimar Constitution; he died in 1920, leaving Economy and Society unfinished.

entries.name: The Spirit of the Laws
entries.desc: The Spirit of the Laws (De l'esprit des lois) is a treatise on political theory and a pioneering work of comparative law by Montesquieu, published anonymously in 1748 after about ten years of work. It argues that political institutions, to succeed, must reflect the social and geographical aspects of the particular community, and pleads for a constitutional system of government with separation of powers, preservation of law and civil liberties. Thomas Nugent published an English translation in 1750, and in 1751 the Church placed it on its Index Librorum Prohibitorum. It influenced Catherine the Great, the Founding Fathers of the United States Constitution and Alexis de Tocqueville.

entries.name: Vatican City
entries.desc: Vatican City is a sovereign city-state, an enclave within Rome, ruled by the pope and governed by the Holy See as the administrative center of the Catholic Church. Catholic theology holds that Saint Peter was crucified on Vatican Hill in the 1st century. The Holy See ruled the Papal States, formed in 756, until the capture of Rome by the Kingdom of Italy in 1870, after which the pope declared himself a prisoner in the Vatican; the Lateran Treaty of 1929 created the modern state. With 0.49 square kilometres and about 882 people it is the smallest country by area and population, and it holds St. Peter's Basilica, the Sistine Chapel and the Vatican Library.

entries.name: The Social Contract
aka: On the Social Contract; or, Principles of Political Right
entries.desc: The Social Contract (Du contrat social) is a 1762 book by the Genevan philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau on how to establish legitimate authority in a political community, one compatible with individual freedom. It argues against the idea that monarchs were divinely empowered to legislate and holds that only the general will of the people has the right to legislate, for only then do the people obey only themselves and remain free. Rousseau separates the sovereign from the government, the executive power, and argues that equality is essential for the attainment of liberty. The book helped inspire political reforms or revolutions in Europe, especially in France.

entries.name: Young Ottomans
entries.desc: The Young Ottomans were a secret society established in 1865 by Ottoman intellectuals who believed the Tanzimat reforms did not go far enough. They sought to preserve and modernize the Empire through constitutional government on the European model, kept rooted in Islam; among them were the writers İbrahim Şinasi, Namık Kemal, Ali Suavi and Ziya Pasha. In 1876 Midhat Pasha conspired with them to overthrow Sultan Abdul Aziz, and Abdul Hamid II reluctantly promulgated the Ottoman constitution of 1876, opening the First Constitutional Era. Abdul Hamid suspended it in 1878, but the Young Turks later repeated their efforts in the Young Turk Revolution of 1908.

entries.name: Dong Zhongshu
entries.desc: Dong Zhongshu was a Chinese philosopher, politician and writer of the Han dynasty, traditionally associated with the promotion of Confucianism as the official ideology of the imperial state. Born in modern Hengshui, Hebei, he rose to high office under Emperor Wu of Han, though he was once imprisoned and nearly executed for writings considered seditious. His thought integrated Yin Yang cosmology into a Confucian ethical framework, and he is considered the originator of the doctrine of Interactions Between Heaven and Mankind, which set rules for the legitimacy of a monarch. The Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals is attributed to him, though scholars doubt much of it is his.

entries.name: Walter Bagehot
entries.desc: Walter Bagehot was an English journalist, businessman and essayist who wrote on government, economics, literature and race. Born in Langport, Somerset, he founded the National Review with Richard Holt Hutton in 1855 and from 1861 edited The Economist for 16 years, widening its reporting of politics. The English Constitution (1867) examined Parliament and the monarchy, and Lombard Street (1873) gave the dictum that central banks in a crisis should lend freely to solvent institutions against sound collateral at high rates, often cited after the 2008 financial crisis. His Physics and Politics (1872) also developed a form of pseudoscientific racism.

entries.name: Amartya Sen
entries.desc: Amartya Sen is an Indian economist and philosopher, born in 1933 in Santiniketan, Bengal, British India, and named by Rabindranath Tagore. He received the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences in 1998 for his contributions to welfare economics, and has also worked on social choice theory, development economics and the measures of well-being of countries. In Poverty and Famines (1981) he argued that famine comes not only from a lack of food but from inequalities in the mechanisms for distributing it. He has taught in England and the United States since 1972, was master of Trinity College, Cambridge, and received the Bharat Ratna in 1999.
